name: Creatine water retention concerns

lead: Creatine is a supplement taken for muscle and strength, and some users worry it makes the face look puffier or softer. Reference sources describe the early weight gain from creatine as water moving into muscle, mainly during loading.

Creatine raises muscle creatine and draws water in by osmosis, which is why muscles look fuller. Long-term studies are described as suggesting it does not necessarily change total body water relative to muscle mass. No study has examined creatine and facial appearance, and user anecdotes conflict.

paras: People take creatine daily in powder form, often with a loading phase at the start, alongside resistance training. Strength and muscle fullness changes are described over weeks. Those watching their face track morning photos and salt intake.

Reviews report no kidney harm in studied groups, though safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy. Early scale weight can rise by water in muscle. People with kidney conditions are generally told to check with a clinician.

chain: Worry about extra water in face
angle.text: Users who take creatine for muscle worry it adds water to the face. Reviews describe the early weight gain as water moving into muscle, mainly during loading, and facial effects have not been studied.

lead: Creatine water retention concerns are worries, common in looksmaxxing and lifting communities, that creatine supplements make the face look puffy or bloated. Creatine is taken to support muscle growth and strength, which feeds a fuller, more muscular physique; the question many users ask is whether the same water-drawing property shows up in the face.[1]

Reference sources describe the early weight gain on creatine as water moving into muscle by osmosis as muscle creatine rises, mainly during the loading phase, and say long-term studies suggest creatine does not necessarily change total body water relative to muscle mass.[1] The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand reports short-term fluid retention of roughly 0.5 to 1.0 litres in early loading studies, proportional to the acute weight gain.[2]
No published study has examined creatine and facial appearance. Users on looksmax.org report mixed experiences, with some describing a puffier face and others noticing nothing.
infobox: About 0.5 to 1.0 L in loading studies

paras: Michel Eugene Chevreul isolated creatine from skeletal muscle in 1832, naming it from the Greek word for meat.[1] Public attention rose around the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, and a strength-focused product, Phosphagen, was introduced by EAS in 1993.[1] Muscle creatine rises by about 20 to 40 percent with supplementation, and performance in repeated high-intensity work improves by roughly 5 to 15 percent.[1]

Creatine's osmotic properties draw a small amount of water into muscle cells. The ISSN position stand reports fluid retention of about 0.5 to 1.0 litres in early loading studies, roughly matching the initial weight gain, and notes that weight gain is the only side effect consistently reported.[2] In one heat study, a week of high-dose supplementation increased intracellular water and reduced cardiovascular and thermoregulatory strain during prolonged exercise.[2]

A 2009 systematic review found no support for concerns about hydration, heat tolerance, cramping or diarrhoea.[1] The ISSN paper states there is no evidence creatine increases dehydration, cramping or musculoskeletal injury.[2]
In a looksmax.org thread, one user asked whether creatine bloats the face; one reply said creatine and minoxidil bloated their face, while another reported no bloating using both.

A 2019 National Kidney Foundation systematic review of 15 studies found creatinine slightly raised but within normal limits and no renal damage, while describing three case reports of renal effects.[1] The ISSN position stand concludes there is no compelling evidence of harm to healthy or clinical groups over up to five years of use, while noting some authors recommend people with existing kidney disease consult a physician first.[2] The ISSN authors report financial ties to supplement companies and the paper was prepared at the request of an industry council.[2]

No studies found on creatine and facial bloating. Studies of body water and creatine are in general populations and athletes: the ISSN review covers short-term fluid retention in loading studies and increased intracellular water in a heat study, and Wikipedia summarises long-term studies as suggesting total body water relative to muscle mass is not necessarily changed.[1][2]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss whether creatine puffs the face, with mixed anecdotes.

claims.claim: Creatine causes no noticeable bloating for some users
